name: Crop Coefficient Calculator
seoDesc: The crop coefficient converts the reference evapotranspiration of a well-watered grass crop into what your crop actually uses: ETc = Kc × ETo. Free crop coeff
summary:
The crop coefficient converts the reference evapotranspiration of a well-watered grass crop into what your crop actually uses: ETc = Kc × ETo. It returns crop water use, crop water use, water per hectare and irrigation needed, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It is the standard first step of irrigation scheduling, and the Kc changes with growth stage, so a maize field in July uses three times the water it used in June. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Crop Coefficient
sections.html:
ETc = Kc × ETo. Irrigation (mm) = ETc − effective rainfall. 1 mm over 1 ha is 10 m³ of water

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
EToreference evapotranspiration of a grass cropmm/day
Kccrop coefficient, a factor by growth stage—
ETccrop evapotranspiration, the water the crop actually usesmm/day

sections.title: How do I use the Crop Coefficient?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the reference evapotranspiration from your weather source, in mm per day.
  2. Enter the crop coefficient for the growth stage the crop is in.
  3. Read the water use in mm and litres per square metre, and subtract any effective rainfall to get the irrigation needed.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: reference evapotranspiration of 5 mm/day, crop coefficient of 1.05, effective rainfall of 0 mm/day.

Substituting them into the formula gives crop water use of 5.25 mm/day, crop water use of 5.25 L/m²/day, water per hectare of 52.5 m³/day, irrigation needed of 5.25 mm/day, irrigation per week of 36.75 mm.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
Kc 0.2 – 0.4Establishmentbare soil and tiny plants lose little
Kc 0.7 – 0.9Developmentcanopy closing, water use climbing
Kc 1.0 – 1.2Mid-seasonfull canopy and maximum water use
above 1.2Very highcertain crops and orchard canopies, or advection

  • ETo is a property of the weather, Kc is a property of the crop, and their product is what the root zone must replace. Keeping the two separate is what makes the method portable between sites.

  • The coefficient is not constant: for most field crops it runs 0.3 early, about 1.0 at full canopy, and 0.5 again at senescence.

  • 1 mm of water over 1 m² is 1 litre. That single identity converts every meteorological figure into a volume you can pump.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Using a single Kc for the whole season instead of the growth-stage values.
  • Treating rainfall as fully effective — heavy storms mostly run off.
  • Scheduling by the calendar rather than by the accumulated ETc since the last irrigation.

faq.q: What is a typical crop coefficient?
faq.a: About 1.0–1.2 at full canopy for most field crops, 0.3 at establishment.

faq.q: How much water is 1 mm of ETc per hectare?
faq.a: 10 m³ — 1 mm over 10 000 m² is 10 m³.
From a local weather network or a reference evapotranspiration service; it is calculated from temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation.

faq.q: What does the Crop Coefficient actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns crop water use, crop water use, water per hectare and irrigation needed. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
